text: ← Foundations contents THE LEARNING PATH WHAT YOU WILL LEARNExplain why a limiting mass appears by comparing pressure exponents and cancelling radius. 01Electron degeneracy pressure survives cooling A white dwarf is supported mainly by electron degeneracy pressure. The Pauli exclusion principle forbids two electrons from occupying the same full quantum state. A spatial state holds at most two opposite-spin electrons, so packing many electrons fills states up to high momenta. What supports a white dwarf?Left: gravity and electron-pressure support. Each right-hand line represents an example spatial state; arrows indicate two spin states. Higher density requires higher momentum states. The lines are not stellar layers and do not reproduce the actual density of states.View larger diagram ↗ For number density nₑ, a spacing scale is d ∼ nₑ−1/3. Counting quantum states gives a characteristic momentum pF ∼ ℏ/d. Uncertainty offers intuition, but does not by itself derive the exclusion principle. pF ∼ ℏne1/3, ne = ρμemu μₑ is mass per electron in units of mᵤ. It is about 2 for fully ionized carbon or oxygen. 02Nonrelativistic electrons give P ∝ ρ5/3 A pressure scale is number density × momentum × speed: P ∼ nₑpv. At low speeds, v ≈ p/mₑ. Insert p ∼ ℏnₑ1/3. PNR ∼ nepF2me ∼ ℏ2mene5/3 ∝ ρ5/3 With ρ ∼ M/R³, PNR ∝ M5/3/R⁵, whereas PG ∼ GM²/R⁴. Shrinking makes degeneracy pressure grow faster, allowing a new equilibrium radius. At fixed composition, balancing the scalings gives R ∝ M−1/3. 03Relativity changes the exponent E2 = p2c2 + me2c4 This energy–momentum relation is an input from special relativity. At p ≫ mₑc, E ≈ pc and v ≈ c. Momentum keeps increasing while speed approaches c. The pressure scaling changes to: PUR ∼ nepFc ∼ ℏc ne4/3 ∼ ℏc(μemu)4/3M4/3R4 04Cancel radius to expose a mass scale ℏc M4/3(μemu)4/3R4 ∼ GM2R4 M2/3 ∼ ℏcG(μemu)4/3 ⇒ M ∼ (ℏcG)3/21(μemu)2 Divide by M4/3, then raise both sides to the power 3/2. Both pressures scale as R⁻⁴, so changing the radius no longer changes their ratio. This is the central reason a limiting mass appears. 05Where does the coefficient near 1.4 solar masses come from? The estimates above deliberately omitted numerical coefficients. We now use the standard result from a detailed structure calculation for a cold, nonrotating, spherical star with ideal degenerate electrons. MCh ≈ 5.83μe2M☉ ≈ 1.46 (2μe)2M☉ With μₑ defined using the atomic mass constant, this ideal model gives about 1.46 M☉, commonly summarized as “about 1.4 M☉.” Different conventions and corrections also lead to values such as 1.44. Composition, electron capture, nuclear reactions, general relativity, and rotation affect real evolution. Crossing a limiting mass does not guarantee one particular explosion. Composition and accretion history help determine whether thermonuclear runaway, collapse, or another outcome occurs. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. In the ultrarelativistic limit, how do degeneracy and gravitational pressure scales change if radius halves? Show the answer and reasoning Both increase by 16, since both scale as R⁻⁴. Shrinking no longer improves pressure support relative to gravity. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS These sources support the laws and numerical values; some use university-level mathematics.
